newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central Africa's president preaches reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: Central Africa's president preaches reconciliation.

text.p: Central African Republic's beleaguered civilian president, Ange-Felix Patasse, preached reconciliation in a New Year message and promised concessions to help defuse the nation's third army revolt in less than a year.
"The resignation of President Patasse remains the only condition for a return to peace," Sergeant Francois Rondossio, one of their spokesmen, told Reuters on Wednesday.

Patasse, in a broadcast to the nation late on Tuesday, promised creation of a committee of national reconciliation by January 15, invited all political groups to join the government and pledged to put an amnesty law before parliament.

He promised municipal elections within three months and also undertook to halt judicial investigations into the activities of the administration of his pre-democracy predecessor, former military leader Andre Kolingba.
"Between now and January 15, the national reconciliation committee will become operational," he said.
A national conference held after a second army revolt in May called for creation of the committee.
"I undertake to place a draft law before the national assembly on an amnesty and I ask my estranged children to come towards me and lay down their arms," he added.
"I no longer want to engage the nation in a spiral of violence," he said. He did not elaborate on the nature of the amnesty or to whom it would apply.
Residents in parts of the city held by mutineers reported gunfire round the time of the broadcast and into the night but the city was calm on Wednesday morning with markets open.
The army mutinies, which began in April, were initially over pay but developed into demands, backed by the opposition, that Patasse step down. Patasse's term of office ends in 1999.
French troops intervened in May under a defence pact to keep Patasse in power. The latest revolt began in mid-November.
Several hundred people have died, many in feuding between Patasse's Baya tribe and Yakomas who dominate rebel ranks.
Four African leaders sent by a Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso in December negotiated a truce, which was extended until January 22, but tension and shooting have persisted.
Troops loyal to Patasse and mutinous soldiers exchanged fire in the capital on Monday after a march by civilians demanding Patasse's resignation. At least 15 people were wounded.

Measures outlined on Tuesday by Patasse, who was elected in 1993 after the country's democratic transition, included broadening access to state media and plans to grant privileges to former heads of state.
Mutineers control suburbs of the capital while loyalists and French troops control the centre.
A team of mediators under Mali's former military ruler, General Amadou Toumani Toure, has been trying to defuse the crisis in the impoverished country.
